fixes.explanation: That's it, baker! Moses and Aaron carry a message to Pharaoh, and the LORD is the one speaking: "But if you refuse to let My people go, I will bring locusts into your territory tomorrow." (Exodus 10:4) Notice the word tomorrow. That's not a vague warning, that's a calendar invite.

Frogs already had their turn, friend (Exodus 8:6). This time the LORD is the one speaking: "But if you refuse to let My people go, I will bring locusts into your territory tomorrow." (Exodus 10:4) I get the mix-up, though. Egypt has had so many plagues that they all start to run together, like batches of cookies on a busy Saturday.
Yes, baker! Right after Moses leaves, Pharaoh's officials speak up. They ask him, "How long will this man be a snare to us?" (Exodus 10:7) I bet somebody had been wanting to say that out loud.

The magicians are a fair guess, friend, but the text names someone else. Pharaoh's officials ask him, "How long will this man be a snare to us?" (Exodus 10:7) So the officials are the ones who speak up next. I think that question had been building for a while.

Nope, baker, Pharaoh's daughter isn't named in this verse. The text says Pharaoh's officials ask him, "How long will this man be a snare to us?" (Exodus 10:7) So the speakers are his officials. Always check who the text actually names.

It's True, friend. Pharaoh's officials tell him, "Let the people go, so that they may worship the LORD their God." (Exodus 10:7) They also ask him, "Do you not yet realize that Egypt lies in ruins?" (Exodus 10:7) That's exactly what the verse gives us, so True is the answer.

That's the one, baker. Pharaoh asks who exactly will be going (Exodus 10:8), and Moses answers, "We will go with our young and old. We will go with our sons and daughters, and with our flocks and herds, for we must hold a feast to the LORD." (Exodus 10:9) He doesn't trim the list at all. Young and old, sons and daughters, flocks and herds. If I had to pack that many for a trip, I'd need a much bigger cookie box.
Not the north, baker, but good effort. The text says "…the LORD sent an east wind across the land." (Exodus 10:13) That east wind blew all day and night. Then morning came with the locusts.

Careful with this one, baker. The text says, "Nothing green was left on any tree or plant in all the land of Egypt." (Exodus 10:15) So a few green plants still being left doesn't match the verse. The locusts came after the hail and ate what the hail had left behind.

Right, baker! The text says the locusts "…consumed all the plants on the ground and all the fruit on the trees that the hail had left behind. Nothing green was left on any tree or plant in all the land of Egypt." (Exodus 10:15) The land was covered until it was black. That's one clean sweep.

That's the word, baker. Pharaoh quickly summoned Moses and Aaron, and then he says, "I have sinned against the LORD your God and against you." (Exodus 10:16) He says it straight to the two of them. I think the locusts got his attention.

Grumbled isn't the word in this verse, baker. Pharaoh quickly summoned Moses and Aaron, and then he says, "I have sinned against the LORD your God and against you." (Exodus 10:16) The word is sinned. That's an admission, not a grumble.

Not this time, friend. Pharaoh asks, "Now please forgive my sin once more and appeal to the LORD your God, that He may remove this death from me." (Exodus 10:17) He's asking them to forgive him and to appeal to the LORD. Telling someone to leave comes later, when Pharaoh says to Moses, "Depart from me!" (Exodus 10:28)

You got it, baker. The LORD sent an east wind that brought the locusts (Exodus 10:13). Then "…the LORD changed the wind to a very strong west wind that carried off the locusts and blew them into the Red Sea." (Exodus 10:19) Same LORD, opposite direction. East brought them in, and west carried them off.

That's right, baker. "Not a single locust remained anywhere in Egypt." (Exodus 10:19) The LORD changed the wind to a very strong west wind that blew them into the Red Sea. Not one was left behind. That's a cleaner kitchen than I've ever managed after a batch.

Not seven, friend. The text says "…total darkness covered all the land of Egypt for three days." (Exodus 10:22) It was three days. I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, so I know a little about long stretches of dark, and three days of it sounds like plenty.

Careful, baker, this is the opposite of what the text says. "Yet all the Israelites had light in their dwellings." (Exodus 10:23) While Egypt was in total darkness, the Israelites had light in their homes. So their homes being dark too doesn't match the verse.

Right, baker! The text says, "No one could see anyone else, and for three days no one left his place. Yet all the Israelites had light in their dwellings." (Exodus 10:23) Egypt couldn't see, but the Israelites had light in their homes. That's a big difference inside one land.

Yes, baker! Pharaoh says, "Even your little ones may go with you; only your flocks and herds must stay behind." (Exodus 10:24) He gives a little on the little ones, but he says the animals must stay. Moses will have something to say about that.

That's the word, baker. Pharaoh says, "Make sure you never see my face again, for on the day you see my face, you will die." (Exodus 10:28) That's a threat on Moses' life, and I think this one hurts. It's one of the heavy lines in the passage.

You got it, baker. Moses answers, "As you say… I will never see your face again." (Exodus 10:29) He answers right after a death threat, and he agrees with Pharaoh. I'd have needed a minute and a few cookies.
